text: Particle-in-cell / PIC Plasma PIC represents a distribution by computational particles and self-consistent fields by a mesh. Its smoothing, collisionality and sampling error differ from direct all-pairs Coulomb dynamics. Problem and representative equations Start with nonrelativistic electrostatic Vlasov–Poisson. Computational particle p has weight wₚ, charge qₚ and position xₚ. Dimensionless shape weights Sᵢ sum to one, and Vᵢ is cell volume. Algorithm Repeat charge deposition, field solution, particle gathering and particle pushing; include background ions in ρ. Electromagnetic PIC additionally needs current deposition and Maxwell updates consistent with discrete continuity. Dawson’s sheet model is a historical particle-plasma example, not the definition of every PIC discretization. Conditions and pitfalls Explicit electrostatic PIC must examine plasma-frequency time scales and Debye-length resolution. Exact restrictions depend on the particle pusher, shape and field solver. Separate sampling convergence in particle count from grid/time convergence, and check self-force and finite-grid heating. The companion is one-dimensional periodic electrostatic cold-electron PIC with a fixed uniform ion background. It is a fixed CIC deposit/gather, Poisson-field and particle-push example; thermal Landau damping, electromagnetic PIC and moving ions are outside its scope. What to check Begin with single-particle self-force, a uniform neutral distribution, and small-amplitude plasma oscillations or Landau damping. Report charge, energy drift, particle-count dependence and independent random realizations. Compare damping rates only within the linear-amplitude regime used by the theory. Use linear cold-plasma oscillation as a small-amplitude reference and vary mesh, time step and particle count separately. Report charge, field residual, self-force, particle momentum and particle-plus-field energy diagnostics separately. Small conservation diagnostics alone guarantee neither trajectory accuracy nor arbitrary long-time stability. The companion also integrates the fixed CIC spatial system with DOP853 and tests tolerance/maximum-step sensitivity. This is an alternative time-integration algorithm, not an independent continuum Vlasov–Poisson solver. The random particle-count check concerns the initial power of one Fourier charge mode, compared with its analytic expectation including the finite-grid CIC response. It is distinct from particle-count convergence of arbitrary nonlinear trajectories. Check fixed inputs: separate scoped releases Check each example’s inputs, observables, diagnostic definitions and scope. What a passing check establishes depends on its acceptance criteria and differs from a general mathematical guarantee. Historical inputs, measurements and criteria are preserved. Cold-plasma oscillation with electrostatic CIC PIC Computation for a fixed target Couple electrons to a 1D periodic grid by CIC, solving Poisson and particle motion self-consistently. Finite amplitude and finite particles leave an error floor. Nonlinear instabilities, Landau damping, collisions, electromagnetic/relativistic PIC and open particle boundaries are unvalidated.
